new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand and group-level only: Nurse & Hinnebusch treat the East Ruvu languages, of which Kwere (their 'Nhwele') is one, as having lost lexical tone/pitch distinctions entirely and as sharing with Swahili an areal penultimate word stress. No Kwere-specific description of stress placement was found; the one first-hand description with a phonology section (Möller 2011) is silent on stress and lists prosody and lexical tone as unstudied.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Kwere; NH1993 hedge that the areal origin 'is not conclusive' and (p. 553) that 'loss of tone/pitch' with stress 'taking over the functions of tone/pitch' is the accurate framing.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level prosody in a comparative-historical survey of Sabaki and its neighbours; the statement is about East Ruvu as a group, based on Google Books snippet view (full pages not opened). Hyman 2017 (p. 161) independently lists Kwere among the toneless Bantu languages but says nothing about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Kwere = Ng'hwele/Ngh'wele (Legère 2021), Nhwele (Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993), Kikwere/Kinghwele (Swahili), Guthrie G32, ISO cwe, Glottolog kwer1261 (East Ruvu > Central East Ruvu). No dialects are distinguished in any source opened; Möller 2011 worked with speakers from Bagamoyo district (Msata area), Legère's list is from the Bagamoyo hinterland. Kutu (kutu1263) and Zalamo/Zaramo (zara1247) are treated by Zahran 2023 as part of one dialect continuum with Kwere.
